tagline.text: Davao's kitchen: an old public market where durian and seafood arrive

location.label: Location
location.text: Bankerohan, Poblacion District, Davao City (around Don Isidro Marfori Road)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: Free entry, spending varies (about ₱200~1,500 is an estimate for fruit, snacks, and souvenirs)

children.text: Bankerohan Public Market is counted among the oldest and largest public markets in Davao City, gathering fish, meat, and vegetables, tropical fruit such as durian, mangosteen, and pomelo, and souvenirs such as malong and banig. There is no entrance fee, and early morning is the liveliest time. It is crowded and pickpockets operate there, so watch your belongings.

Bankerohan Public Market is a large traditional market in the Poblacion District of central Davao City. The city tourism office describes it as "one of the oldest markets in the city," and a 2005 local article called it a "landmark" of the city. It is one of Davao's three large public markets (Bankerohan, Agdao, and Toril) and the large one in the urban center, and the same article put its area at about 1 hectare. I could not confirm its exact founding year. In a September 2025 local report, a city councilor said the market earned about ₱60.7 million in 2024. That suggests a market of this size and age still contributes meaningfully to city finances, so it helps to know it is a different kind of place from a souvenir-shop tourist attraction.

This is less a tourist attraction than a place where Davao's daily life is on view. According to older sources, fish trucks arrive in the small hours of the morning to unload fish from General Santos, and vegetables from Kidapawan are traded in a wholesale area on the sidewalk. That is why the best time to visit is described as the morning, especially early morning, when the goods are fresh and the sound of bargaining is liveliest. Older records say vegetable wholesale ran for about two hours in the early morning and about five hours in the late afternoon. The market has a ground floor and a second floor, the second floor once had bulalo stalls, and reports say some vendors moved upstairs after the 2024 demolitions. Fish, meat, vegetables, clothes, and shoes are sold in separate areas. Where each area is can change, so it helps to take a first lap around the market to get your bearings.

The fruit stalls are what travelers should look for. Davao is famous for durian, and the market sells not only durian but also mangosteen, pomelo, and candied fruit. Durian prices vary greatly with supply, and a 2023 local report even expected prices to more than double as the harvest season wound down. Dried fish, chili and spices, snacks such as chicharon and fish crackers, wooden ladles and spoons, and souvenirs such as malong and banig are sold as well.

Recently there has been talk of renovating the market. In 2022 a cashless QR payment system (Paleng-QR Ph) was introduced at the market, and in May 2024 stalls occupying the roads and sidewalks around it were demolished. In September 2025 a city councilor proposed improving the second floor and opening a pasalubong (local products) center, but this is still only a proposal. So keep in mind that the layout and shop locations at the time of your visit may differ from these sources.
Durian, mangosteen, pomelo, and candied fruit are piled high. Durian prices vary greatly by variety and season, so compare several stalls and check the condition before buying.

blocks.title: Pre-dawn fish unloading and wholesale area

children.text: According to older reports, fish trucks arrive in the early hours of the morning to unload and sort the catch, and vegetable wholesale on the sidewalk ran in the early morning and late afternoon. Current operating hours need confirming, but you only see the most market-like scene in the morning. Many vendors carry loads and push carts, so do not block the way.
Some eateries inside the market are known to sell soup dishes such as bulalo and instant coffee. A simple meal in the market is the cheapest way to eat, but choose by looking at the hygiene yourself.

Wooden ladles, spoons, forks, old kerosene lamps, and fabrics such as malong and banig are sold. Old records say prices were lower than at souvenir shops near hotels, but check whether that is still true by bargaining.

In March 2025, as part of the Araw ng Dabaw celebrations, the Davao City tourism office held a Bankerohan walking tour introducing the market's history, vendors, and crafts. I could not confirm whether it runs regularly, so check the tourism office's announcements.
Many stalls do not have fixed prices, so bargaining is common. One guide says some vendors even add extra goods, so bargaining with a smile is the closest way to enjoy the local atmosphere.
Arrive by Grab or taxi and start with the fruit stalls near the entrance.
Walk through the vegetable and fish areas and watch the vendors' morning scene and stall layouts.
Have a simple breakfast and coffee at an eatery inside the market.
Buy fruit and snacks, and browse the souvenir stalls for malong or wooden tableware.
Wash your hands and head to your hotel or the next stop (the cathedral or a downtown cafe).

Exact opening hours differ from guide to guide, so it is safest to confirm locally. If it is your first visit, it is easy to get lost inside the market, so agree on a meeting point with your group beforehand, and if a guided walking tour is offered, consider joining it.

items.title: Half-day Davao route
items.subtitle: Combine the market with downtown sights

children.text: Browse the fruit and snacks at Bankerohan Market and have breakfast.
Take a taxi toward San Pedro Cathedral and look around.
Have lunch at a restaurant downtown and rest.
Return to your hotel to sort out the fruit you bought, or continue with a trip nearby.
Flights run from Manila to Francisco Bangoy International Airport (DVO) in Davao. Airlines and schedules change by season, so check when you book.
From the airport to the city center, use a taxi, Grab, or hotel pickup. The travel time depends on traffic.
From a downtown hotel in Davao, Grab or a taxi is the easiest option. Traffic around the market is heavy, so going early in the morning is much easier.
The market is in the central Poblacion District, with several jeepney and tricycle routes passing, but routes change often, so check locally.

Even after the 2024 demolitions, the area around the market is crowded with vendors and vehicles mixed together. When taking a taxi, decide where to get off in advance, and watch traffic carefully when crossing roads.
Explore the inside on foot. The aisles are narrow and the floor is wet, so non-slip shoes are best.
Vendors and vehicles are mixed on the surrounding roads and sidewalks, so keep checking your surroundings as you walk.

The market is open all year, and within the day, the morning, especially early morning, is liveliest and the goods are freshest. Midday is hot and crowded, and older sources say vegetable wholesale ran for about two hours in the early morning and about five hours in the late afternoon. Around holidays and paydays it is said to be more crowded with shoppers, so choose a weekday morning if you want a relaxed visit.

Durian has the greatest variety and steadier prices in harvest season, but the season differs from year to year, so check locally. In the rainy season the market aisles get muddy, so boots or sandals are better, and during the Kadayawan Festival in August the whole city can be crowded.

Bankerohan is a market, not accommodation, so it is easier to stay in central Davao. From downtown hotels you can get there easily by taxi or Grab. The area around the market has many old shops and street stalls and gets quiet at night, so it is best not to linger there late at night. Davao can be confusing on a first visit, so if you plan to combine the market with sightseeing in one day, staying in the city center (around Poblacion) cuts travel time.

You can eat at the eateries and street stalls inside the market. Soup dishes such as bulalo, coffee, and fresh fruit are the standards, and if you have a sensitive stomach, start with packaged snacks or fruit with a peel. Hygiene differs from shop to shop, so choose places many people visit. One guide says you can also buy gift fruit at other fruit stalls near the market. To eat market fruit at your hotel, bring a knife and plastic bags or ask the vendor to peel it for you. Durian is often restricted in where you can eat it, so it is simplest to eat it at a shop near the market.
Early mornings are cooler.

a kilo for Puyat durian. Before buying, ask which variety it is, the price per kilo and whether the weight includes the husk.
Bring cash in small bills. Some shops accept QR payments, but not all.
Start bargaining with a smile, and check the weight after you agree on a price.
Durian has a strong smell and may be banned in hotels and on transport, so check before buying, and it is easiest to eat it on the spot.
Bring non-slip shoes for the wet floor, and a small umbrella or hat.
Wear your bag in front and keep your phone and wallet out of sight.
Do not carry large bags around, and browse lightly, buying only what you need.
Ask vendors for permission before taking photos.
After browsing, wash your hands or bring wet wipes, and wash fruit at your hotel before eating.
If you bought a lot of fruit, check weight and packaging, and check your airline's rules if you will carry it on a plane.
It is a crowded traditional market with pickpockets and petty thieves. Leave valuables at your hotel and keep your belongings in front of your body.
Older sources pointed to cleanliness and order as problems and a lot of garbage. Check for yourself whether this has improved when you visit.
Reports say some vendors who moved to the second floor after the May 2024 stall demolitions had low sales, so some stalls may be empty or have moved.
The aisles are narrow and the floor is wet and slippery. Watch your step.
Choose street food by its hygiene, and be careful with ice and raw food, which can upset your stomach.
Hours differ between guides, with some saying 24 hours and others saying early morning to late afternoon. I could not confirm the official hours.
Strong-smelling fruit such as durian is sometimes banned in hotels and on transport, so check before you buy.
Davao City
is the city where this market stands, with restaurants, cafes, and parks throughout the center.
San Pedro Cathedral, Davao
is a downtown church close to the market, and works well as a follow-up after a morning market visit.
The
Philippine Eagle Center
, a little way out of the city, is a good follow-up for a nature-focused day.
